Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack earlier this week
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, Russia has said.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.
The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.
A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November
It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China .
Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram.
Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge.
"As a result of a nighttime drone attack, train services on the railway section of the Crimean Bridge have been temporarily suspended," the ministry said in a statement on Telegram.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.
At least four people were killed in a Russian drone attack on the southern city of Odesa on Wednesday, according to Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.
That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.
Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.
Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse
A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami . He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.
Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas , Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.
CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.
By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.
Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.
But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.
So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."
The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.
Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.
It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.
The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.
Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.
Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.
So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?
At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".
The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.
It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.
"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."
What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.
It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.
Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?
"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.
"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."
So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.
But these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.
It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.
There is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.
It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.
With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.
Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.
Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.
If Anthropic – and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.
While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.
Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.
He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.
That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of new more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.
But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it – the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development – means that buying interest is high.
It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.
With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is likely given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.
Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are currently back to $145.
The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.
Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.
"Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."

Prosecutors accused Christian Emmanuel Sanon of seeking to replace then-Haitian president Moise.
A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship has been convicted in the United States on charges stemming from the assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise, following a nearly eight-week trial in a federal court in Miami.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon, 68, was found guilty on Wednesday on all eight charges, including conspiring to kill the Caribbean nation’s president, who was shot dead in his home on July 7, 2021.
Prosecutors said in court records that the scheme to kill Moise, 53, included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programmes that were intended to help businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic.
They said South Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moise and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing.
Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moise, but said the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill the president and maintained his innocence throughout the trial.
He was arrested in Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, days after the assassination. According to a report by local police seen by the Reuters news agency, when officers searched his residence, they found eight vehicle registration plates, 19 passports and 12 mobile phones, as well as 30 boxes of ammunition and 12 pistol holsters.
Moise’s widow, Martine Moise – a key witness in the trial – was flown to Florida for treatment for bullet wounds she sustained in the attack. She has now registered as a presidential candidate for Haiti’s 2027 general election , the first in more than 10 years.
Sanon, who remains in federal custody, showed little reaction as the jury verdict was announced. He faces up to life in prison and is set to be sentenced on February 10.
His attorney, Zeljka Bozanic, said the defence team was disappointed and would file an appeal at the appropriate time. Prosecutors declined to comment after the verdict.
US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination, and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
A new list of indictments released by US prosecutors in September included four people whose names were redacted.
Seven more people have been charged for their roles in facilitating the funding of the assassination plot and helping those responsible evade justice after the killing, including Vitel’homme Innocent, a gang leader tied to the kidnapping of 17 US and Canadian missionaries later in 2021. He has yet to be arrested.
Those still to face trial include Joseph Felix Badio, a former government anti-corruption official whom other suspects’ defence lawyers have accused of masterminding the operation, and 17 Colombian former soldiers flown in from Haiti in September.
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers impersonating US Drug Enforcement Administration agents killed Moise and injured his wife in a night-time raid on their home outside Port-au-Prince.
A series of transitional governments followed, as armed gangs, widely believed to be aided by corrupt politicians, seized control of much of the capital and surrounding regions.
The United Nations Human Rights Office documented 4,595 people killed in armed violence between January 1 and October 31 this year.
The situation has caused economic, security and humanitarian crises, forcing nearly 1.5 million people to flee their homes, according to the UN.

Sotheby's staff handle the "Châtaigniers en fleurs" painting by Vincent van Gogh at an auction preview in Hong Kong last month
Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (£144.8m).
The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.
The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.
Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.
The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.
Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.
Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.
"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.
The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Caracas on Wednesday, announcing a resumption of military cooperation with Venezuela and vowing to crack down on drug traffickers. The trip marks the highest-level US visit since the ouster of Nicolas Maduro in January, signalling a dramatic shift in relations between the two countries.
Embattled US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced appearance in Caracas on Wednesday, the highest-level US visit since the January ouster of president Nicolas Maduro .
During the surprise stopoff en route to Colombia , Hegseth announced renewed US-Venezuelan military cooperation and vowed to "hunt" down drug traffickers.
"We will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you," he said after announcing the deal that marks a dramatic thaw in long-hostile relations.
"You will no longer export your crime and your misery to America, to Venezuela , or any other country in the region," he added, referring to "narco-terrorists."
Venezuela's interim leader Delcy Rodriguez hailed a "resumption of the technical-military relationship between both countries" after years of rupture and US sanctions .
She has governed Venezuela with Washington's backing since US special forces captured Maduro and spirited him to New York , where he faces trial on charges of "narco-terrorism."
Read more Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro and wife Cilia Flores deny US torture charges as 'false accusations'
The American embrace of Maduro's former vice president has not gone down well among the country's often-repressed pro-democracy opposition.
While Venezuelans enjoy more freedoms than a year ago, US President Donald Trump 's administration has allowed swaths of the authoritarian state apparatus to remain in place.
Hundreds of political prisoners remain behind bars and no date has been set for free and fair elections .
But Venezuela is seen as vital for US efforts to secure new sources of oil, isolate Cuba 's communist government and curb cocaine trafficking from South America.
Caracas has long been accused of harboring Colombian drug-running guerrilla groups including the ELN, which operate across vast tracts of territory on either side of the border.
Hegseth, who recently avoided congressional impeachment and faces sustained scrutiny for his handling of the Iran war and the legality of deadly anti-drug strikes, later traveled to the Colombian capital Bogota.
Read more Rubio kicks off tour in Latin America as US vies for regional influence
Since Trump returned to office two years ago, the United States has significantly escalated military operations in Latin America.
US forces have struck alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, killing more than 230 people, according to an AFP tally.
Rights groups say Trump's administration has provided scant proof that the vessels had anything to do with drug trafficking , warning that the strikes may amount to extrajudicial killings.
Washington has deployed troops, powerful Reaper drones and other military assets to the region.
AFP uncovered at least 20 US military flights to an isolated base on Ecuador 's Pacific coast, including C-130 Hercules and C-17 Globemaster transport planes, V-22 Osprey tiltrotor aircraft and Black Hawk helicopters.
Satellite imagery shows the base undergoing significant construction work in recent months.
The US has also backed anti-narcotic strikes in Colombia , where Hegseth landed on Wednesday.
Washington and Bogota have long counted each other as allies in the war on drugs, with one governing the world's biggest cocaine market and the other its largest producer.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has sought to deepen the relationship even further since his inauguration in August, boosting military cooperation with the US and bombing drug-running guerrillas.
More than 300 US soldiers recently took part in anti-drug-trafficking exercises in the country alongside 400 Colombian soldiers.
Defence Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora, who greeted Hegseth in Bogota, announced the visit on Tuesday along with the delivery of a C-130 military aircraft.
The defense secretary's trip follows an impeachment attempt by Congress that threatened his job less than two years into his tenure.
Analysts say that when the Democratic majority is sworn in in January, Trump's policies and his Latin American alliances will come under fierce examination.

Critics hail GTA 6 as a ‘masterpiece’, ‘spectacular’, and an ‘astonishing American epic’.
Grand Theft Auto VI has launched to rave reviews, in one of the most hotly anticipated releases in gaming history.
Gamers got their hands on the latest instalment of the GTA franchise on Thursday, as critics hailed the open-world game as a “masterpiece”, “spectacular”, and an “astonishing American epic”.
The immersive game had an aggregate score of 99 out of 100 on Metacritic, based on more than 150 reviews, as it began dropping on game consoles worldwide from midnight.
“Exquisitely detailed, endlessly ripe for experimentation, and uncompromisingly engineered, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played,” critic Luke Reilly wrote in a gushing review for gaming website IGN.
“Accepting that GTA 6 is very much not real also makes it all the more astonishing how much the game is very real,” reviewer Jordan Minor wrote in PCMag.
Grand Theft Auto VI follows the exploits of Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, a Bonnie and Clyde-like duo who become entangled in a criminal conspiracy after a seemingly easy score goes awry.
Players have free rein to explore the hyper-realistic fictional state of Leonida and its coastal metropolis of Vice City, stand-ins for Florida and Miami.
Like previous entries in the series, Grand Theft Auto VI features graphic depictions of crime and violence, with players able to mow down pedestrians in stolen vehicles and engage in shootouts with police.
The game, developed by New York-based Rockstar Games at an estimated cost of more than $1bn, is the first instalment in the series since the release of Grand Theft Auto V in 2013.
Originally set to go on sale in 2025, the release was delayed twice to allow developers to polish up gameplay.
Grand Theft Auto VI, which is available on the PlayStation 5 and the Xbox Series, is likely to be the most lucrative release in the history of the gaming industry, which is projected to be worth as much as $350bn by the end of the decade.
Pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto VI exceeded an estimated 15.8 million units as of November 17, generating $1.54bn in revenue, according to the market intelligence platform Sensor Tower.
The GTA series began in 1997 with the launch of Grand Theft Auto, a 2D top-down open-world game available on the personal computer, PlayStation and Game Boy Color.

Bayesian, which sank off Sicily killing seven including tech tycoon, had not been fully assessed, say investigators
The superyacht Bayesian, which sank in a storm off Sicily killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter, was vulnerable to knockdown but crew were not aware as it had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down, the final report from the UK’s Marine Accident Investigations Branch (MAIB) has said.
The 56-metre (184ft) vessel was anchored near the fishing port of Porticello when it sank during a violent storm shortly before dawn on 19 August 2024.
Lynch, 59, had been enjoying a voyage around Sicily with family and friends after his acquittal in a long-running fraud case regarding the sale of the technology company he founded, Autonomy, to Hewlett-Packard in 2011.
He and his 18-year-old daughter, Hannah, died, as did lawyer Chris Morvillo and his wife, Neda, banker Jonathan Bloomer and his wife, Judy, and the yacht’s chef, Recaldo Thomas. Nine other crew members and six guests were rescued.
The MAIB final report, published on Thursday, appears to contrast with recent reports from Italy , where prosecutors have reportedly blamed errors by the crew.
The MAIB report details how the yacht was hit “by extreme winds that were not explicitly forecast” of about 70 knots (80 mph), which knocked it on to its side in less than 15 seconds. It sank 18 minutes later.
Investigators found that the yacht’s vulnerability to strong winds had never been assessed for the conditions in which it was anchored, with its sails down and its retractable centreboard raised. The centreboard is a large underwater structure that helps a sailing vessel remain stable.
The extreme weather was most likely caused by a downburst – a powerful blast of air from a thunderstorm that hits the sea and spreads out with enormous force, the report said.
None of the life rafts on board automatically inflated or released from the vessel. The crew managed to release one manually. Survivors were rescued by crew from a nearby yacht, the Sir Robert Baden-Powell.
Rob Loder, the chief inspector of MAIB, said: “This accident developed with extraordinary speed. In just 14 minutes, calm conditions had given way to winds of at least 68 knots, which in less than 15 seconds pushed the yacht on to its side.
“Our investigation found that Bayesian had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down. The extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk.”
The report conveys the desperate minutes as the Bayesian was knocked down. Crew were alerted by sudden and severe winds of up to 30 knots at 03.55, and within two minutes the yacht listed starboard and the vessel began to drag anchor before the wind suddenly increased to about 70 knots.
“At 04.06 Bayesian violently heeled over 90 degrees to starboard, taking less than 15 seconds to do so. People, furniture and loose items fell across the deck. The generators shut down immediately and battery-supplied emergency lighting automatically turned on,” the report said.
Some guests, awoken by the listing and who had left their cabins, escaped. One couple used furniture drawers as an improvised ladder. Guests who managed to get to the flying bridge were instructed to swim away from the vessel and warned to stay clear of the mast and boom as it sank.
Passengers and crew who made it out gathered in the water, using a torch on a mobile to search for others. A crew member managed to swim back to the yacht to manually release one life raft from stowage. By 04.24 the life raft was inflated.
The investigation found that, with no sails set, Bayesian was vulnerable to knockdown in severe winds. This vulnerability was affected by its loading condition, apparent wind angle and the position of the centreboard, but had not been identified in the originally approved stability information available to the crew.
It said information contained in guidance provided to mariners did not provide sufficient detail of the impact of possible weather conditions to support decision-making. The weather forecast also did not indicate the risk of downbursts from the thunderstorms it predicted, it said.
Inquest proceedings in the UK are looking at the deaths of Mike and Hannah Lynch and Jonathan and Judy Bloomer, who were all British nationals.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.
In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."
The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.
I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission , external .
I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.
But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.
Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled across the Myanmar border in 2017 as attacks on them grew
The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.
Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".
A UN report in 2018 , based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.
As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.
Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.
It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.
This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.
Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.
Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, was responsible for the military's operations in 2017
The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.
She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.
Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.
Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.
Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.
When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.
Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.
Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.
Aung San Suu Kyi's refusal to condemn the Myanmar military's actions in Rakhine State dismayed her admirers
But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar.
"What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government's language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 'clearance operations'," Suleman said.
"We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel - all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent."
What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia?
Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed "the crime of crimes", as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica.
That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military's operations in 2017, and who has been trying to improve his dismal international image in recent months.
There is no right of appeal against an ICJ verdict. However, there is also no penalty that follows an ICJ verdict.
The Burmese coup leader is focused mostly on rebuilding relations with neighbouring Asian countries, who are unlikely to pay too much attention to such a verdict, and much less on rebuilding relations with Western countries who do care.
Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar mark the ninth anniversary of their exodus from Myanmar
But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada.
"For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year."
He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety.
More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up.
Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back.
Many Rohingya villages have been completely destroyed. And international support for them has faded over the years. Even an unprecedented genocide verdict at the world's highest cou…

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela on Wednesday, state TV reported, during an unexpected visit to Caracas.
Hegseth was received by Venezuela's interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, in the capital ahead of a planned visit to Colombia later Wednesday.
"We see this as a renewal of our defence partnership and an opportunity for our two great armed forces to work together," Hegseth said, according to footage broadcast by VTV, Venezuela's state television channel.
The trip, which had not been publicly announced by the Pentagon, marks another step in the rapprochement between Washington and Caracas following the capture in January of Nicolás Maduro.
The cooperation agreement announced by Hegseth and Rodríguez provides for the resumption of technical and military cooperation between Washington and Caracas, which had been suspended for years amid deteriorating diplomatic relations between the two countries.
According to the Venezuelan leader, one of the main objectives is to strengthen the training of Venezuelan armed forces personnel through joint training and cooperation programmes. Rodríguez said the initiative would help improve the military's preparedness to respond to shared threats.
The agreement also aims to improve the operational equipment available to Venezuelan forces and provide access to new technologies. So far, neither government has provided details on the timeline for implementing the agreement, the resources to be allocated or the specific mechanisms through which cooperation will take place.
Rodríguez took power after Maduro was captured, although her continued leadership of the country remains shrouded in uncertainty. Her interim mandate expired in July and there is still no announced date for the next presidential election.
The rapprochement between Washington and Caracas has also been marked by agreements over Venezuelan oil and by the United States' strategy against drug trafficking in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which has caused the deaths of at least 240 people since September 2025 in attacks on vessels suspected of carrying drugs.
Hegseth's visit is part of efforts by Donald Trump's administration to expand its influence in Venezuela. The defence secretary is the third member of Trump's cabinet to travel to the country this year, following trips by the interior and energy secretaries, focused on Venezuela's oil and mineral resources.

The autonomous driving company suspended driverless taxi rides on US highways days after California banned the vehicles on its own freeways
Waymo has stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways across the US indefinitely. The Alphabet subsidiary pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after California banned them from freeways in response to recent traffic incidents.
Waymo had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin. The California-based company offers rides on city streets in many other areas, including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver. Those rides remain unaffected by suspended freeway service.
A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an email that the company has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service”, though it’s “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel”. The suspension was implemented last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they didn’t say how long it would last.
Waymo’s voluntary suspension came the same day as the California department of motor vehicles banned the company’s robotaxis from the state’s freeways. The ban followed two traffic incidents, including one in which three Waymo driverless vehicles drove into a construction zone, a DMV spokesperson, Jonathan Groveman, said in a statement.
The construction zone incident occurred on 5 November, and the second incident, which involved California highway patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.
Video of the 6 November incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.
“The department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.
Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on 18 May.
The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions”.
California’s restrictions bar Waymo from operating and testing its driverless vehicles on the state’s freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions”.

There were 22 people on board the Bayesian at the time of the incident
The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about a critical safety risk that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily, killing seven people, British investigators say.
British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024.
The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.
Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.
"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."
The accident also led to the deaths of Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71; American lawyer Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57; and crew member Rick Thomas , 59.
The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about a critical safety risk that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily coast, killing seven people, British investigators say.
British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024 .
Mike Lynch and his daughter Hannah both died when the Bayesian sank
Rob Loder, chief inspector of marine accidents said: "Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of the seven who lost their lives, and with all those affected by the loss of Bayesian. This accident developed with extraordinary speed."
Fifteen survivors escaped from the 56-metre (184ft) luxury yacht and managed to get to a life raft that had been launched by a crew member.
The marine investigation found that the Bayesian "had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down".
In addition, "the extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk", Loder added.
In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.
With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).
The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.
A study commissioned by the MAIB indicated that, in the conditions assessed, Bayesian was vulnerable to extreme winds at the vessel's widest point, known as the beam.
It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.
The wreackage of the Bayesian off the coast of Porticello, Sicily
In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.
Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.
They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.
The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.
Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.
The MAIB's final report into the sinking, published on Thursday, appeared to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecution experts have reportedly blamed errors by the crew rather than problems with the yacht.
The investigation was carried out alongside a criminal probe in Italy , where captain James Cutfield, chief engineer Tim Parker Eaton and deckhand Matthew Griffith are under investigation over potential charges of multiple manslaughter and culpable shipwreck.
British investigators said that Italian prosecutors had restricted access to some witnesses and evidence.
"It is possible that the circumstances depicted in this report may alter following disclosure of evidence withheld by the Italian authorities," the report says.
However, the MAIB's Graves said he was satisfied with the British investigation.
"We are content with our investigation, the investigation that we've undertaken, and the information we've used to feed into it."
The report also found that alcohol consumption had not contributed to the sinking.
MAIB investigator Simon Graves: "This was an accident and there were a number of contributory factors"
The MAIB report makes seven recommendations to four agencies. It calls for new regulations to be set for single-hulled sailing vessels, and new rules around life rafts.
It also urges collaboration between the Met Office and its global counterpart to improve information-sharing of severe weather forecasts with mariners.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

A Russian national has been arrested in California on suspicion of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defence company that provided support to Ukraine, US officials said on Wednesday.
Igor D'iu faces charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, operating as a foreign agent without notifying US authorities, stalking and fraud.
"Igor D'iu was allegedly recruited, directed, and funded by the Russian government to stalk employees of a major US technology company," Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said in a statement.
Rozhavsky said D'iu used "physical surveillance, electronic tracking devices, and fraudulent identities to gather intelligence."
US Attorney Craig Missakian said the company was targeted because of its "assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia."
"We will not tolerate any efforts -- by foreign governments or otherwise -- to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," Missakian said.
According to the indictment, D'iu travelled from Turkey to Mexico in June 2026 before being smuggled into the United States, where he allegedly communicated with his Russia-based co-conspirators via Telegram.
They allegedly instructed him to gather information on company employees and visit a coffee shop near its Palo Alto office to "photograph their laptop screens while they worked."
FBI agents found $18,000 (€15,500) in cash, a fake US passport under the name "Hugo Landry Johns" and two Russian passports during an October raid on D'iu's home in East Palo Alto, according to the Justice Department.
If convicted, D'iu faces up to 10 years in prison for acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the US attorney general, five years for conspiracy, five years for stalking and one year for fraud.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq20:
The alleged foreign agent was discovered with two Russian passports
A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supports the Ukrainian military.
Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a covert operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. The BBC understands that the company targeted was Palantir Technologies.
D'iu is also charged with stalking employees and possessing falsified identity documents.
The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia.
"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.
"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."
Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.
He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".
On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.
He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.
His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".
The suspect allegedly took photos of employees screens at a cafe near the office
A source in the industry confirmed that Palantir was targeted, and added that the operation did not penetrate the company's private systems.
They added that the company has been "targeted extensively" by Russia over its involvement in Ukraine, and that the attacks are becoming "increasingly aggressive".
The source, who did not want to be named, said that this was the first time a Russian operative was found while on US soil attempting to spy on the company.
"I think the surprising thing is that they decided to take the risk of sending someone to the US," they said, in an attempt to get into the system "physically".
Palantir has not issued a statement in reaction to the charges.
D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.
On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.
During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".
A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.
He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.
The suspect was found with forged identification documents including a US passport
Ukraine's long-range drones using Western tech to hit Russia
He has been held in jail since 2 November. It is unclear whether he has hired a lawyer who can speak on his behalf.
Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.
The arrest comes as espionage allegations roil the US tech industry, amid the news that Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.
Last month, a former OpenAI employee was charged with planting a listening device in a company office. The man was later accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government.

Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.
The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will be in the majority.
His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the Senate also being under Democrats' control.
Jeffries told reporters after the vote that the nomination was "a high honour and a distinct privilege".
As of Wednesday, Democrats will hold at least 257 seats in the House next year, which is well beyond the 218 needed for a majority. Seven races from the recent midterm elections are still uncalled.
Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.
The Congressional Black Caucus, currently made up of only Democratic House members, noted the potential history-making moment when Jeffries takes the helm of the House.
"The American people, largely driven by turnout among Black communities, particularly across the south, have trusted us to make Washington work for them," said the committee's chair, Yvette Clarke, in a statement. "Now, it is our charge and responsibility to do all we can to deliver on their faith."
Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote , Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change.
"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.
All congressional Democrats are gearing up for clashes with the White House once they officially take control in January.
President Donald Trump, a Republican, has signalled a willingness to work with Democrats on some issues, but has also pledged to use his veto power to reject legislation he does not like.
Trump's opposition could make it hard for Democrats to deliver on their campaign promises to address affordability and pass other reforms.
At a news conference following the vote on Wednesday, Jeffries pledged that House Democrats would "fight to lower the high costs of groceries and gas and housing", and "make healthcare affordable for every single American".
Though the party will have a large enough majority to weather defections on must-pass legislation, Jeffries will still have to navigate internal ideological divisions that have grown particularly sharp over US support of Israel and Americans' rising healthcare costs .
Many incoming Democrats, including members of the Democratic Socialists of America, won their elections by challenging the party establishment.
The Congressional Progressive Caucus, from the party's left wing, congratulated Jeffries on the nomination, adding they would "continue conversations with Leader Jeffries to ensure Democrats deliver a bold agenda for working people".
Along with shepherding legislation, Jeffries as Speaker will also have to manage the complex array of investigations that Democrats plan to launch into Trump, his family, and cabinet members now that they have regained control of the chamber's oversight powers.
Rounding out their party leadership team, House Democrats also elected Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as majority leader, Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip, and Joe Neguse of Colorado as assistant speaker.

The Gambia accused Myanmar of genocide following a 2017 military crackdown displacing over 730,000 Rohingya.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, is set to rule in a landmark case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority.
The reading of the judgment will begin at 10am (09:00 GMT) on Thursday at the Peace Palace in The Hague and is expected to last up to 90 minutes.
It could be the first time the court rules that a state has committed genocide.
The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, but the court has very limited means of enforcing it. If Myanmar ignores it, The Gambia could ask the UN Security Council to act.
The Gambia, a Muslim-majority West African country, brought the case in November 2019 with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
It argues that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide resulting from a 2017 military offensive that drove at least 730,000 Rohingya, who are mostly Muslim, from Buddhist-majority Myanmar into Bangladesh.
Survivors have recounted killings, mass rape and the burning of villages. A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the campaign included “genocidal acts”.
Myanmar denies genocide and says its forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups. It argues there is no direct evidence of an intent to destroy the Rohingya.
Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires proof of the specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
The ICJ has never held a state responsible for committing genocide. In 2007, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, but ruled that Serbia had not itself committed genocide.
The judgment could also set precedents for other cases, including South Africa’s case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
The ICJ settles disputes between states, so it can find Myanmar responsible but cannot try individuals, which is the duty of the International Criminal Court.
The Gambia has asked the ICJ to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible, make reparations and ensure the Rohingya can return safely . Myanmar disputes The Gambia’s right to seek reparations on their behalf.
About 1.2 million Rohingya live in the Cox’s Bazar refugee settlement in Bangladesh, where many will follow the judgment, the Reuters news agency reported. Roughly 550,000 remain in Myanmar, with restrictions on their movement, healthcare and livelihoods.

Assessment of damage is underway, days after two attacks that destroyed road section of key bridge across Kerch strait linking annexed peninsula to Russia
A key bridge connecting annexed Crimea to Russia has been attacked again, a Russian-appointed regional governor has said, two days after Ukrainian strikes caused serious damage to it.
“Following a new attack on the Crimean Bridge, traffic has been temporarily halted. All relevant services are on site and at work. An assessment of the damage is under way,” Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea , wrote on Telegram. The Russian transport ministry said on Thursday that no one was wounded in the attack and that train services across it had been halted.
Wednesday’s ‌attack is third this week on the highly symbolic bridge that links Russia with Crimea, which ​it seized from Ukraine in 2014. A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed this week, but the rail corridor appears to be operable despite sustaining some damage.
The strike came just hours before an unprecedented meeting between Russian president Vladimir Putin and his Chinese and American counterparts, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, in China. One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said this week’s attacks were designed to embarrass Putin on the world stage. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.
For Ukraine, the bridge is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge across the Kerch strait, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried twice to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
Earlier, Ukraine critically damaged the road section of the bridge in what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation . A span of the bridge’s road section collapsed, but the railway line was still standing.
Zelesnkyy described the earlier attack as the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles. Palianytsia drones hit the road section of the bridge, while Neptune and other missiles targeted the adjacent rail section, he added.

World court to issue key verdict in its first genocide ruling in more than a decade.
The top court of the United Nations is scheduled to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority in a case brought by the West African nation of The Gambia.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague is to deliver its verdict on Thursday in what will be its first judgement on the merits of a genocide case in more than a decade.
Legal experts said the ruling could bear on South Africa’s ongoing case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza, which Israel is contesting.
The Gambia accuses Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people during a 2017 military crackdown that forced hundreds of thousands to flee. Myanmar, meanwhile, claims it was responding to attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) on police posts.
Myanmar’s military began what it called clearance operations in Rakhine State in October 2016 and a far larger campaign in August 2017 after attacks on police posts by a Rohingya armed group. About 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 740,000 forced to flee to Bangladesh, the UN estimated.
UN investigators found that soldiers razed hundreds of villages, carried out mass killings and routinely raped and gang-raped Rohingya women, girls and boys. They said the sexual violence indicated genocidal intent.
The military itself has announced convictions in only two cases brought after the violence. However, in one, seven soldiers jailed for killing 10 Rohingya men and boys at Inn Din village were freed after serving less than a year of their 10-year sentences.
In 1982, long before the crackdown, Myanmar excluded the Rohingya from its 135 recognised ethnic groups, calling them immigrant Bengalis despite many families having lived in Myanmar for generations. Nearly all Rohingya have been denied citizenship since then, making them the world’s largest stateless group .
Since fighting with the military resumed in 2023, the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group, has taken most of the state. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights said in August that both forces have committed widespread and systematic abuses against the Rohingya, accusing the Arakan Army of torture, sexual violence and forced recruitment.
The UN said those abuses have driven more than 155,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh since early 2024, taking the refugee population there up to about 1.2 million.
Nearly all the refugees live in crowded camps in the Cox’s Bazar District, where they are dependent on international aid that has fallen sharply in recent years, particularly since United States President Donald Trump’s administration slashed foreign aid in 2025. Most refugees now receive smaller food rations, and many camp schools have closed. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees warned that recent arrivals often lack sufficient food, clean water and healthcare.
The Gambia said it brought the case after decades of persecution of the Rohingya that culminated in the 2017 operation, which it argued breached the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The Muslim-majority nation of 2.5 million people filed the case in November 2019 on behalf of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). The case was led by Abubacarr Tambadou, then The Gambia’s attorney general and justice minister.
In January 2020, the court ordered Myanmar to take emergency measures to prevent genocidal acts.
Myanmar initially argued that The Gambia, which was not directly involved in the conflict, could not bring the case. But in 2022, judges ruled that it could because both countries are parties to the convention, under which all signatories are obligated to prevent and punish genocide.
Hearings on the merits of the case followed in January this year with seven states – including Canada, France and the United Kingdom – backing The Gambia.
The judges must decide whether Myanmar, as a state, committed genocide against the Rohingya, thereby breaching the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.
The ICJ passes judgements on state actions. It does not rule on the criminal guilt of individual soldiers or commanders.
Under the convention, “genocide” refers to acts such as killing and causing serious harm committed with intent to destroy, wholly or partly, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
Evidence that a state has committed atrocities is not enough. The court must also find they were carried out with specific intent to destroy a group. Such intent can be shown through direct statements or orders or inferred from a pattern of conduct.
The Gambia argued that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference from Myanmar’s conduct.
Myanmar, meanwhile, said it was conducting a legitimate counterterrorism operation against Rohingya fighters, not targeting Rohingya people as a whole.
A genocide finding would formally recognise the harm the Rohingya have suffered but may do little in the short term for the more than one million victims of violence and displacement, said Michael Becker, an international law professor at Trinity College Dublin and a former ICJ legal officer.
The Gambia wants the court to order Myanmar to ensure displaced Rohingya can return safely to their land, compensate them, and replace or rebuild destroyed homes and property.
Becker told Al Jazeera the court may impose those demands only partly or in general terms, leaving Myanmar to decide how to comply with them.
Such an outcome would “surely be disappointing” to those who are sceptical that the government would fulfil those demands in good faith, he said.
“Even if the ICJ were to order far-reaching forms of relief, the political conditions on the ground in Myanmar are not amenable to realising that relief anytime soon,” Becker said.
He said a finding would instead have to be used to pressure Myanmar diplomatically.
William Schabas, an international law professor at Middlesex University in the UK, said the measures that The Gambia was seeking on behalf of the Rohingya were “robust” even though they fell short of demanding citizenship, which would end their statelessness.
“Assuming Myanmar implements the conclusions, this will indeed have significant positive effects on the security, dignity and livelihoods of the Rohingya in Myanmar,” Schabas told Al Jazeera.
The Myanmar ruling will be the first final judgement out of five genocide cases pending before the ICJ.
Becker said the outcome could clarify the court’s longstanding “only reasonable inference” test. Under it, judges infer genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct only if no other reasonable explanation fits.
He said the court’s two rulings on the Balkan wars left it unclear whether genocide could be deemed to occur alongside armed conflict, which he said was “an unduly restrictive standard”.
Thursday’s judgement could instead treat armed conflict as an alternative explanation for a party’s conduct, rather than an automatic bar to establishing genocidal intent, he said.
According to Schabas, the ruling will “have very dramatic effects” on the outcome of the other pending cases, particularly the case against Israel.
“In my opinion, the South African case against Israel is much stronger than the case of Gambia against Myanmar. If Gambia wins against Myanmar, we can be confident that South Africa will prevail over Israel,” he said.

Pierce Brosnan, yeni açıklanan yedinci Bond Robert Pattinson'ı "yolculuğun tadını çıkar" diyerek seçkin 007 kulübüne karşıladı.
Pattinson'ın pazartesi günü yeni James Bond olarak açıklandığı duyurusu, Daniel Craig sonrasında serinin geleceğine dair yıllardır süren spekülasyonlara son verdi.
Brosnan, Bond'u canlandıran beşinci oyuncuydu ve 1995 yapımı GoldenEye ile başladı. Ardından üç filmde daha rol aldı: Tomorrow Never Dies (1997), The World Is Not Enough (1999) ve Die Another Day (2002).
Brosnan, bugün erken saatlerde yaptığı bir Instagram paylaşımında Pattinson'ın "muhteşem" bir Bond olacağını söyledi.
Brosnan, şunları yazdı: "Sevgili Robert, Bond dünyasına hoş geldin. Muhteşem olacaksın. 'Remember Me'yi birlikte çekerken geçirdiğimiz zamana dair güzel anılarım var. Olağanüstü bir külliyat yaratmanı ve adım adım güçlenmeni izlemek büyük bir mutluluk oldu."
Brosnan ve Pattinson, 2010 yapımı romantik drama filmi Remember Me 'de birlikte rol aldı.
Brosnan, sözlerini şöyle tamamladı: "Yolculuğun tadını çıkar. Grá mor, Pierce."
Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner ve Nicholas Hoult'un da aralarında bulunduğu oyuncuların, Pattinson'ın açıklanmasından önce rol için adaylar arasında olduğu bildirildi . Pattinson, beyazperdede James Bond'u canlandıran yalnızca altı oyuncunun, Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Brosnan ve Craig'in, izinden giden isim olacak.
Brosnan daha önce Turner'a desteğini açıklamıştı ve bu hafta başında, yaşayan en yaşlı 007 oyuncusu Lazenby de Pattinson'ı ekibe hoş geldin diyerek karşıladı.
1969 yapımı On Her Majesty's Secret Service 'de Bond'u bir kez canlandıran 87 yaşındaki oyuncu, Instagram'da bir video mesaj paylaştı.
"Robert, dünyadaki en seçkin kulübe hoş geldin," diyen Lazenby, ardından şu tavsiyeyi verdi: "Ama eğlenmeyi unutma. Bakalım senin de 'bu diğer adama hiç olmadı' anın olacak mı."
Lazenby, sözlerini "Her şey gönlünce olsun dostum, George" diyerek tamamladı.
Serinin 26. Bond filmi geliştirme aşamasında, yönetmen koltuğunda Denis Villeneuve, senaryodan ise Steven Knight sorumlu.
Çekimlerin gelecek yıl başlaması bekleniyor. Ancak Pattinson'ın, yönetmen Matt Reeves'in kişisel bir sorunla karşı karşıya kalması üzerine yapımı geçici olarak durdurulan The Batman Part II 'nin çekimlerini tamamlaması gerekiyor. Son birkaç haftanın çekilmesine yardımcı olmak için Steven Soderbergh devreye girdi.
Bu da, izleyicilerin yeni Bond macerasını en erken 2028'in ikinci yarısında görebileceği anlamına geliyor. Böylece Daniel Craig'in veda filmi No Time To Die 'den bu yana yedi yıl geçmiş olacak ve Bond filmleri arasındaki süre, 1989 tarihli Licence To Kill ile 1995 tarihli GoldenEye arasındaki dönemden bu yana görülen en uzun arayı oluşturacak.

Milyonlarca çalışanın gözü, aralık ayında toplanacak Asgari Ücret Tespit Komisyonu'na çevrildi. 2027'de cebe girecek rakama ilişkin tahminler netleşmeye başlarken SGK Uzmanı Özgür Erdursun da canlı yayında konuştu. Erdursun, asgari ücret için zam oranını verdi.
TGRT Haber'deki canlı yayında 2027 asgari ücret zammına ilişkin soruları yanıtlayan Özgür Erdursun, beklentisini açık bir oranla ortaya koydu. Erdursun, 'Yüzde 25 gibi artış bekliyorum açıkçası' diyerek masadaki en olası senaryonun bu olduğunu ifade etti.
Bugün net 28 bin 75 lira olan asgari ücrete yüzde 25 zam yapılması halinde yeni rakam yaklaşık 35 bin 94 liraya ulaşıyor. Erdursun da hesabı yuvarlayarak 'Ben düz 35 bin lira olacağını düşünüyorum' dedi. Uzmana göre rakamın üst sınırı ise 36 bin lira civarında kalacak.
36 bin liralık bir asgari ücret, mevcut tutara yaklaşık yüzde 28'lik bir zam anlamına geliyor.
Erdursun tahminini yaparken enflasyon tarafındaki tabloya dikkat çekti. 2026 için yapılan yüzde 27'lik artışın ardından yıl sonu enflasyonunun yaklaşık yüzde 30 seviyesinde kapanmasının beklendiğini hatırlatan Erdursun, aradaki farkın asgari ücretlinin cebinde yaklaşık 3 puanlık bir kayba dönüşeceğini söyledi.
2027 için belirlenen enflasyon hedefinin yüzde 21 olduğunu vurgulayan uzman, zam oranının bu kayıp da hesaba katılarak belirlenmesi gerektiğini anlattı. Yüzde 25 beklentisi de bu iki rakamın arasından çıkıyor: Hedef enflasyonun üzerine geçen yılın kaybı eklendiğinde ortaya çeyreklik bir artış oranı çıkıyor.
Erdursun'un altını çizdiği bir diğer nokta ise fiyat artışlarının kalıcı olarak frenlenmesi oldu. Uzman, 'Önemli olan enflasyonu dizginlemek' sözleriyle asıl meselenin zam oranının ötesinde olduğuna işaret etti.
Erdursun, tahmininin yanı sıra dikkat çeken bir ihtimale de değindi. Uzmana göre seçim takviminin yaklaştığı bir dönemde, Ocak 2027'de hem emekli aylıklarında hem de asgari ücrette beklenmedik iyileştirmeler gündeme gelebilir.
Erdursun daha önce Dünya gazetesindeki köşesinde yüzde 25 ile yüzde 35 arasındaki senaryoları masaya yatırmıştı. Canlı yayındaki açıklamasıyla bu aralığın alt bandına yakın bir rakamı öne çıkarmış oldu.
Asgari Ücret Tespit Komisyonu'nun aralık ayında toplanması bekleniyor. Yeni rakamın ay sonuna doğru açıklanması ve 1 Ocak 2027'den itibaren geçerli olması planlanıyor.
